# System Intent and Design Life Cycles


Hardware and software complexity has outpaced what manual design loops can explore, and computer architecture has answered that kind of pressure before by advancing its design methods alongside its devices. Part I sets out the ambition of Architecture 2.0, explains why manual design loops are under pressure, and organizes the work an AI-native design system would have to do, without assuming the ambition is met or moving the commitment away from a named architect.

The immediate tension is that generative models and search methods can propose candidates far faster than simulation, formal verification, and expert review can evaluate them, so generation on its own creates no engineering value. Part I names that asymmetry, follows the Lighthouse prompt as it expands into eight coupled requirement domains, and organizes the resulting search into a staged life cycle that routes each failure back to the stage that owns it.

::: {.callout-part}
1. How can compact system intent become a verifiable cross-stack architecture without diluting system obligations or human commitment authority?
2. Why does candidate generation outpace verification capacity, and where does that gap limit the design loop?
3. How should an AI-native design life cycle route repairs to the stage that owns them and keep a reviewable record across stage boundaries?
:::

## Governing Design Principles {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Each chapter in Part I states one governing design principle. Together they anchor automated exploration in claims that can be checked, in the resource that limits progress, and in stage boundaries that send a failure to its owner rather than into the global search state:

- **@sec-moonshot:** Expand Expressible and Checkable Space. An architecture moonshot succeeds when it enlarges the design intent a team can express and binds that intent to repeatable, independent verification, not when it raises the rate at which candidate artifacts appear.
- **@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales:** Relieve the True Limiting Constraint. Identify whether exploration, evaluation, verification, or review limits the next architectural decision, and aim assistance at that work without moving the burden downstream.
- **@sec-architecture-20-ontology:** Isolate Failure Domains for Repair. Independently failing outputs belong to distinct responsibilities, and an inadequate result routes back to the responsibility that owns its repair rather than restarting the whole study.

## Chapter Roadmap {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The three chapters of Part I move from compact architectural intent to a design life cycle another architect can review. @tbl-part-i-roadmap organizes the architecture question and the deliverable of each chapter:

| **Chapter** | **Core Architecture Question** | **Key Takeaway / Deliverable** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **@sec-moonshot** | What system-and-chip design capability is Architecture 2.0 trying to create, and what would count as achieving it? | Defines the moonshot, the three operational layers of AI in design, the eight requirement domains the Lighthouse prompt expands into, the difference between a generated artifact and an architecture result, and commitment authority. |
| **@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales** | Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance help? | Explains how complexity, verification demand, and evaluation cost compound, defines the design loop and the design path it is distinguished from, and locates where point AI assistance might relieve the limiting constraint. |
| **@sec-architecture-20-ontology** | Once an AI-native design system is being considered, how should the work be organized, and why does that structure matter? | Establishes the six-stage life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), how repairs route back to the stage that owns them, and the study record and Design-Loop Card that keep a question coherent across stages. |
: **Part I chapter roadmap across intent, physical pressures, and life cycle staging.** The opening chapters set the ambition, explain the pressure on manual design loops, and organize the work into stages that keep commitment with a named architect. {#tbl-part-i-roadmap tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Together, these three chapters set the standard that every method, representation, and environment in the rest of the book must meet. Part I begins in @sec-moonshot with the Lighthouse prompt and the moonshot it names.
